A job is due a period after its latest run on record started, whoever started that run, and at once when it has no run on record. A run an operator starts therefore moves the schedule: the next run is a period after it. A run that fails counts as well, and the next is a period later.

When a job is due the manager reads its latest run once more and, if a period has passed, has a run started on one of the nodes that hold the system jobs, taking the nodes in turn. The node answers once the run is on record. A node that does not answer is followed by the next one, once the recorded runs show that no run was started.
A job that comes due while its latest run is still executing is refused its run, as any run of an exclusive job is, and is due again a period later. The manager logs a warning naming that run.

A job whose latest run cannot be read, whose run no node started, or whose run was refused while its latest run on record is not executing, is due again a minute later. The other jobs keep their schedules.
After the manager's node fails, or the whole cluster restarts, a job that came due meanwhile runs once, however many periods passed.
Periods are constants in code. During a rolling upgrade the manager schedules the jobs of the node it sits on; once that node restarts, its next host schedules its own.
